## Biography & Recruiting Context

Isaac Vazquez is a second-year MBA candidate at UC Berkeley Haas, Class of 2027, looking for a full-time role in product management, product marketing, or program management that starts after he graduates in May 2027, and he is interested in consumer tech broadly.

At Civitech, a campaign software company, his QA role grew into product work. He owned the product vision for the TextOut texting platform, led a pricing initiative that generated $4M in additional revenue in 2024, and helped launch RunningMate. In summer 2026 he was the MBA growth intern at Juno, a fintech company that negotiates group rates on student loans, focusing on funnel conversion analysis and member activation. He is a Consortium Fellow and MLT Professional Development Fellow, and he builds and maintains the tools on this site.

---

## Working Principles & Philosophy

### 1. Check what produces the number
Before acting on a metric, understand the query or event instrumentation behind it. At Juno, correcting one click event moved the funnel's biggest drop off a step earlier, to members who had an approved rate and never clicked through to a lender.

### 2. Watch customers use the real thing
Alpha demos work best when customers work through their actual workflows in new builds. At Civitech, alpha demo observation revealed the messaging window was cutting off message content, leading directly to a user story, business case, and a production fix within one week.

### 3. Put the limits next to the number
A simple comparison can easily mislead. At Juno, advising meetings superficially appeared to multiply conversion, but most occurred after the conversion they were credited with. Building a matched estimate showed the true causal lift was a fraction of the headline number.

## Representative Articles & In-Depth Writing (Full Text)


### Agentic AI in Plain English: What It Is and Why Product Managers Should Care

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/agentic-ai-explained-for-product-managers
- Published: 2026-04-08
- Topic: Agentic AI
- Excerpt: I use agentic AI to mean systems that take a goal, plan intermediate steps, use tools, and continue until a task is done. Those abilities change how I think about permissions, failure handling, and product evaluation.

The word agent has gotten stretched far enough that it now means almost nothing on its own. I hear people use it for chatbots, copilots, workflow tools, and fully automated systems that can go take actions across several applications. That is too much ground for one word to cover. If I am being precise, I use agentic AI for systems that can take a goal, decide on intermediate steps, use tools to execute those steps, and keep going long enough to finish meaningful work without a human having to drive every turn.

That last part matters more than the branding language around it. A chatbot can sound smart and still be non-agentic in any useful sense. If I have to keep choosing the next step, pasting in the missing context, and telling it which tab to open or which source to check, I am still doing the workflow myself. The model is just helping me talk through it. An agentic system earns the name when it can hold onto the objective, move through a sequence of actions, and return with something closer to completed work than a single answer.

When I explain the distinction to PMs, I usually start with the job rather than the model. If the job is "answer my question," a chatbot may be enough. If the job is "research three competitors, compare pricing changes, pull examples, and draft a brief I can react to," then the question becomes whether the system can plan, call the right tools, recover when one of them fails, and show me what it did. That is the practical difference. I do not think it helps to turn this into abstract taxonomy when the product consequences are concrete.

## Key takeaways

- **Agentic AI definition**: Systems that receive a high-level goal, plan intermediate steps, operate external tools (APIs, code, search), and iterate until the task is complete without human micro-steering.
- **The four production pillars**: Autonomous path planning, external tool execution, multi-turn state preservation, and inspectable audit trails.
- **The product manager's focus**: The core design challenge shifts from response quality to permissions, execution boundaries, failure recovery, and safe human-in-the-loop escalation.
- **Common failure mode**: Products that market general autonomy while silently degrading or getting trapped in loops on non-ideal tool responses.

## What makes an agentic system feel real

The systems that feel meaningfully agentic to me usually have four things working together. They can decide on an execution path instead of just continuing the conversation. They can use external tools that matter, whether that is search, code execution, a database, or an internal API. They keep enough state to avoid starting over every few minutes. And they expose the work in a way that a human can audit when something looks off.

I think PMs often focus on the first part and underweight the other three. Planning is the flashy part in demos. Tool use, state management, and recovery are where production products either become trustworthy or fall apart. A system that can make a plan but cannot reliably operate the tools it needs is just a confident narrator. A system that can use tools but cannot preserve context across a longer workflow becomes exhausting to supervise. A system that can do both but hides its actions behind a polished chat bubble will eventually create a trust problem of its own.

That is why I do not find "it feels like ChatGPT but for workflows" to be a useful product description. Once a system can act, the interface and control model matter much more than they do in a pure Q and A product. The product is no longer just about quality of generated language. It is about visibility, reversibility, permissions, escalation, and the point at which the user is supposed to step back in.

## Why PMs should care about the distinction

PMs need to understand this because the design questions change the minute a system is allowed to do more than answer. The important questions are no longer just "Was the response good?" and "Did the user get value?" They become "What was the system allowed to do?" "How did the user know what was happening?" "What happened when the agent got something wrong?" and "Could the user stop it before a small error became a real one?"

I think this is where a lot of AI product thinking still feels shallow. Teams treat an agent like a stronger assistant and then act surprised when users ask for an audit trail, a confirmation step, or a cleaner handoff to a human. Of course they do. Once the system can act on their behalf, the emotional contract is different. People do not calibrate trust in agents the same way they calibrate trust in autocomplete. If the product does not make that legible, the user either overtrusts it or never trusts it enough to use the feature seriously.

The PM who understands planning, tool use, memory, and interface design at a practical level has a much easier time pushing the right conversations forward. You do not need to be the person implementing orchestration logic. You do need enough depth to ask whether the workflow actually needs autonomy, whether the tool definitions are solid, whether the review points are in the right places, and whether the user can recover cleanly when the system does something dumb. Those are product questions, not just engineering questions.

## What I think the current products get wrong

Most agentic products are still better in a narrow lane than they are across a wide one. That is not a criticism so much as a design constraint. The systems I trust most are the ones that do less, more clearly. They are explicit about their tools, explicit about their limits, and explicit about where a human should step in. The ones I trust least are the ones that advertise general autonomy while quietly depending on ideal inputs, ideal data, and ideal tool responses.

So where does that leave PMs? In my mind, the practical takeaway is simple. Do not ask first whether a product has an agent. Ask what work it can finish without supervision, what systems it can touch, how it handles failure, and what the user sees while it is doing the job. If the answers to those questions are weak, the product is probably less agentic than the marketing suggests. If the answers are strong, you are looking at a genuinely different product surface, and it deserves to be designed that way.

If you want the adjacent pieces, [Build vs Buy for Agentic AI: When Startups Should Roll Their Own](/writing/build-vs-buy-agentic-ai-platform) is where I think through the platform decision, and [How I'd Evaluate an Agentic AI Product as a PM (Interview-Ready Framework)](/writing/evaluate-agentic-ai-product-pm-framework) is the cleaner framing for assessing whether an agentic product is actually designed well.

### How I'd Evaluate an Agentic AI Product as a PM (Interview-Ready Framework)

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/evaluate-agentic-ai-product-pm-framework
- Published: 2026-04-10
- Topic: Agentic AI
- Excerpt: I evaluate an AI agent product by whether the task fits, what actions the system can take, how failures reach a human, and whether the result can be measured. In a PM interview, those are the questions I would work through first.

When a PM interview turns to agentic AI, the candidates who struggle usually make the same mistake. They reach for a general product framework and start talking about growth, retention, engagement, and competitive landscape as if the product were just another SaaS surface with a language model inside it. None of those things are irrelevant. They just are not the first things I care about.

If I am evaluating a candidate on an agentic AI question, I want to know whether they understand what is uniquely fragile about products that can act, not just talk. I want to hear whether they question the task fit, whether they understand trust as a design problem, and whether they know how to talk about failure without getting vague. Those are the signals that tell me the person has actually thought about this category and is not just swapping AI terminology into a standard PM answer.

## The first questions I would ask

The first question is whether the task even deserves an agentic product shape. That is the simplest test and the one people skip most often. Does the job require multiple steps, tool use, longer-running execution, or action on the user's behalf. Or is it really just a conversational assistance problem wearing more ambitious language. Candidates who ask that question early usually understand scope better than candidates who take the agentic premise as given.

The second question is what the user is being asked to trust. I think this is the center of the evaluation. If the system can act, then predictability, transparency, and control matter immediately. Can the user tell what the system is doing. Can they stop it. Can they understand why a result happened. Can they recover when the agent took the wrong branch. If a candidate cannot talk concretely about that, the rest of the analysis usually sounds polished but hollow.

The third question is how the product fails. I care a lot less about whether someone can recite a metrics stack than whether they understand the difference between an obvious failure and a silent one. An agent that visibly fails is annoying. An agent that quietly makes the wrong move and leaves the user thinking it succeeded is much more dangerous. When a candidate starts talking about loops, bad actions, weak escalations, invisible errors, and audit trails, I pay attention. That person is closer to the actual problem.

## What I would listen for in a strong answer

A strong answer usually gets more specific as it goes. On metrics, for example, I would want to hear something beyond standard retention language. I want to hear task completion quality, escalation timing, override rate, and where human correction is showing up. I want to hear that the candidate knows a zero escalation rate is not automatically good and that a high completion rate may hide low-quality completions. Those are category-specific instincts, and they matter.

I also want to hear a view on differentiation that is more durable than "the model is strong." That answer was weak a year ago and it is weaker now. What matters more is workflow context, proprietary data, tool access, integration depth, and whether the product is learning from repeated use in a way a generic agent cannot. Candidates who say that plainly usually understand that the product moat is not the same thing as the model vendor's moat.

The interview-ready version of all of this is not a memorized checklist. It is a way of showing how you think. Start by questioning task fit. Move quickly into trust and failure design. Use metrics that actually reflect agent behavior. End with what the product owns that is hard to copy. If I heard that shape from a candidate, I would take it seriously, because it tells me they know where these products succeed and where they get exposed.

### 4-Pillar Agentic Evaluation Rubric

| Evaluation Pillar | Core PM Evaluation Question | Green Flags (Ready to Scale) | Red Flags (High Risk of Failure) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Task Boundedness | Does the workflow require autonomous tool use, intermediate verification, and bounded state changes? | Closed-loop state space, deterministic check steps, scoped API permissions | Open-ended creative tasks with unbounded search spaces |
| 2. Trust & Control Surface | Can the operator inspect the thought-trace, interrupt execution, and undo mutations? | Explicit preview states, granular approval gates, continuous audit trail | Black-box execution, silent irreversible writes, all-or-nothing autonomy |
| 3. Failure & Recovery | What happens when an external tool fails or the agent branches off course? | Fast escalation timeouts, explicit fallback modes, deterministic schema guards | Silent hall-of-mirrors hallucination, runaway loop spend, unmonitored completions |
| 4. Defensibility & Moat | Where does long-term competitive advantage accrue as foundation models improve? | Proprietary context stores, domain-specific evaluation testbeds, low-latency tooling | Pure wrapper over public LLM APIs without unique state or feedback |

That is also more or less how I evaluate real agentic products. The interview framing is different, but the substance is the same. I am not looking for a clever framework name. I am looking for evidence that the person understands the product surface, the failure surface, and the human trust problem well enough to make good decisions once the product leaves the demo. For scoring product bets on impact, confidence, effort, and reversibility, I built the [Decision Lab](/decision-lab).


If you want the pieces that sit around this framework, [Agentic AI in Plain English: What It Is and Why Product Managers Should Care](/writing/agentic-ai-explained-for-product-managers) is the cleaner category primer, [What an AI Agent Actually Costs in Production](/writing/what-an-ai-agent-actually-costs-in-production) breaks down the unit economics, and [AI Agents for Customer Support: What Actually Works in 2026](/writing/ai-agents-customer-support-what-works) is a concrete example of how the trust and failure questions change once the workflow gets real.

### What an AI Agent Actually Costs in Production, From Someone Who Pays the Bills

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/what-an-ai-agent-actually-costs-in-production
- Published: 2026-05-14
- Topic: Agentic AI
- Excerpt: An AI agent makes repeated model calls as it works through a task, so its cost depends on the number of steps, the context carried into each call, and retries. I look at those costs per completed task, along with caching and limits on how long a run can continue.

There is a conversation happening on a loop right now between finance teams and product teams, and it goes like this. Finance says token prices have fallen something like ninety percent in two years, so why did our AI spend triple? Product says usage grew. Both are telling the truth and neither has actually explained the bill. I run agents at small scale for my own projects and have watched the same dynamics at much larger scale, and I want to lay out where agent costs actually come from, because the mental model most teams carry, price per token times tokens per request, is the wrong one, and it produces forecasts that miss by multiples.

The core issue is that an agent is not a request. A chat completion is one model call with a bounded input and output, and per-token math describes it fine. An agent is a loop. It reads context, calls a tool, reads the result, decides, calls another tool, and iterates until done, and every iteration re-sends an expanding context window. Two things about that loop break naive cost models. The iteration count is variable and unbounded by anything except your configuration, and the context grows as the loop runs, which means cost per step rises through the task. A task that takes three steps and a task that takes thirty are the same product feature with an order of magnitude between their costs, and you mostly do not control which one a given user request turns out to be.

What I found instrumenting my own workflows is that the distribution of cost across tasks is brutally skewed. The median agent run is cheap and getting cheaper, exactly as the falling token prices promise. The tail is where the money goes. The run that hits a confusing error and retries its way through forty steps, the research task that pulls in ten large documents and then carries them through every subsequent call, the loop that gets stuck and burns its entire step budget before failing. A small fraction of runs routinely accounts for the majority of spend, which means your average cost per task is nearly useless for forecasting and your tail behavior is everything. Budgeting agents on average cost is like budgeting a hospital on the average patient.

## Key takeaways

- **Loops vs. requests**: Chatbots are single requests with bounded token cost; agents are iterative loops where expanding context increases the cost per step.
- **Tail-skewed economics**: Average cost per task is misleading because median runs are inexpensive, while long, retrying, or stuck loops in the tail drive the majority of the monthly bill.
- **The four cost levers**:
  1. *Prompt caching*: Massive savings on repeated system prompts, tool definitions, and conversation histories.
  2. *Model routing*: Frontier reasoning models for planning and recovery; efficient models for mechanical data formatting.
  3. *Context compaction*: Aggressively summarizing tool returns to prevent quadratic token growth.
  4. *Step budgets*: Strict, non-negotiable iteration ceilings to eliminate infinite runaway loops.

## The levers that actually move the bill

So what moves the number? In rough order of how much they have mattered in practice, for me and for the production deployments I have seen up close.

Caching is first and it is not close. Agent loops re-send the same system prompt, tool definitions, and accumulated history on every iteration, which makes them close to the ideal case for prompt caching. Both [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) and [Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) document prompt caching as a direct way to reduce repeated-input cost and latency. An agent that structures its stable context to maximize cache hits can cut spend without changing the product behavior at all. This is the single most boring and most effective line item in agent economics, and teams skip it because it is plumbing rather than strategy.

Model routing is second. The instinct to run the whole agent on the frontier model is understandable, because the frontier model fails least, and a failed run is wasted spend plus a retry. But most agent loops contain a lot of low-judgment steps, formatting results, extracting fields, deciding whether a tool result is an error, and routing those to a model that costs a twentieth as much is nearly free quality-wise. The pattern that has settled in is a strong model for planning and recovery, a cheap model for mechanical steps. Where I would push back on the cost-cutting instinct is downgrading the planner, because a worse planner produces longer loops, and longer loops eat the savings. Cheaper steps, yes. Cheaper judgment, usually a false economy.

Context discipline is third, and it compounds with both of the above. Every tool result you let into the window gets paid for on every subsequent step, so verbose tool output is not a one-time cost, it is a subscription. Summarizing or truncating results before they enter the loop, and compacting history as tasks run long, attacks the quadratic-ish growth that makes long runs disproportionately expensive. This is the same context engineering work that improves output quality, which is a happy alignment. The cheap agent and the good agent are substantially the same agent.

And then there are step budgets, which are less a cost optimization than a survival requirement. Every production agent needs a hard ceiling on iterations and spend per task, because the failure mode of an agent without one is not a bad answer, it is an unbounded bill attached to a stuck loop. Set the ceiling, log what hits it, and treat every budget-exhausted run as a defect to investigate, because the tail of your cost distribution is made entirely of these.

Where does this leave the unit economics question? In a much better place than the panicked version of the conversation suggests, honestly. Falling token prices are real, caching is real, routing is real, and an agent feature that was uneconomic eighteen months ago is frequently viable now with the same architecture and a quarter of the cost. What has not arrived, and what I would stop waiting for, is the version where costs are low enough that you can stop thinking about them. Agents convert money into iteration, and products built on them need someone who understands the loop well enough to know which iterations are worth buying. That is not a finance question. That is the product job now.

For the model-selection side of that decision, [Reasoning Model Economics](/writing/reasoning-model-economics-when-to-use-which) is the more tactical comparison. [The New Model Economics](/writing/new-model-economics-tier-collapse-2026) covers why the architecture now matters more than a simple price-per-token table.

### Context Engineering Is What Prompt Engineering Wanted to Be

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/context-engineering-replacing-prompt-engineering
- Published: 2026-03-12
- Topic: Agentic AI
- Excerpt: Context engineering is deciding what information a model sees when it answers, from retrieved documents to tool results and task history. I think selection, compression, freshness, and source authority matter more than most prompt wording changes.

Two years ago, prompt engineering was being sold as a career. There were courses, certifications, job listings with the phrase in the title, and a small cottage industry of people sharing magic incantations that supposedly made models behave. I was skeptical of most of it at the time, and I think that skepticism has aged well. The wording of an individual prompt matters far less than people claimed, and it matters less every time models get better at understanding intent.

But something real was hiding inside that hype, and it has a better name now. Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what information a model has access to at the moment it produces an answer. Not how you phrase the request. What the model can actually see. After a year of building agent workflows for my own projects and watching teams ship them at work, I would argue this is the single highest-leverage skill in AI product development right now, and it is almost entirely unrelated to the prompt-wording tricks that used to dominate the conversation.

## Key takeaways

- **Context vs. prompt phrasing**: Prompt wording matters less as models improve; context engineering—controlling the exact data, tools, and history a model sees—dictates production output quality.
- **Context rot**: Irrelevant context is never neutral; it actively degrades model attention and reasoning quality over extended workflows.
- **Four core context operations**: Selection (tight retrieval filters), compression (compacting histories), freshness (stamping and aging documents), and source hierarchy (resolving contradictory data).
- **Production reality**: In multi-step loops, step fifteen is dominated by accumulated tool returns; engineering that history is where reliability is won or lost.

## Why the framing shifted

The shift happened because the systems changed. When the interface was a single question and a single answer, the prompt was the whole input, so obsessing over its wording made a kind of sense. Agent systems broke that model. An agent running a twenty-step task is accumulating context the entire way. Tool results, file contents, earlier reasoning, error messages, retrieved documents. By step fifteen, the original instruction is a small fraction of what the model is looking at, and the quality of the output depends on the quality of everything else in the window.

What I found building my own agent workflows is that almost every failure I initially blamed on the model was actually a context failure. The agent that confidently used a stale API signature had a six-month-old document in its retrieval set. The agent that lost track of the task halfway through had a context window full of verbose tool output burying the instruction. The agent that contradicted itself was carrying two conflicting versions of the same fact from different sources, with no signal about which one to trust. None of these get fixed by rewording the prompt. All of them get fixed by changing what the model sees.

There is a name floating around for the degradation that happens when context windows fill up with low-quality material, and I think context rot is the right one. Models do not weigh every token in the window equally, and they do not gracefully ignore irrelevant material. Irrelevant context is not neutral. It actively competes with the relevant context for the model's attention, and past a certain point, more information makes answers worse. The teams that internalize this build very different systems from the teams that assume a bigger window means you can stop curating.

## What the work actually looks like

So what does context engineering involve in practice? In my experience it comes down to a handful of decisions that most teams make implicitly and badly, and that good teams make explicitly.

The first is selection. Of everything you could put in front of the model, what earns a place? The instinct is to include everything that might be relevant, because leaving something out feels like the bigger risk. I think that instinct is wrong most of the time. A retrieval system that returns the three most relevant documents will usually beat one that returns fifteen, even though the fifteen contain more total information, because the model's effective attention is a scarce resource and you are spending it either way.

The second is compression. Long-running agents have to summarize their own history or they drown in it. The [OpenAI compaction guidance](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction) treats compaction as a first-class way to reduce context size while preserving the state needed for later turns. The interesting design question is what survives the summary. A good compression step preserves decisions, constraints, and open questions while discarding the play-by-play. A bad one preserves the play-by-play and loses the constraint that actually mattered, which is how you get an agent that re-litigates a decision it already made an hour ago.

The third is freshness and authority. When two pieces of context conflict, which one wins? Most systems have no answer to this, so the model improvises, and it improvises inconsistently. The fix is structural. Date your documents, rank your sources, and make the hierarchy explicit in how context gets assembled. This is boring data plumbing, and it moves output quality more than any prompt revision I have ever made.

What is interesting here is how little of this resembles the prompt engineering era. Nobody is debating whether to say please. The work looks like information architecture, retrieval tuning, and pipeline design. It looks like engineering, because it is.

### Prompt Engineering vs. Context Engineering

| Architecture Dimension | Prompt Engineering (2023–2024) | Context Engineering (2025–2026) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Primary Focus | Phrasing, tone modifiers, few-shot prompt templates | Dynamic token pipelines, retrieval hygiene, context budget allocation |
| Core Mechanism | In-context steering via prose formatting | Programmatic selection, history compaction, metadata re-ranking |
| Execution Horizon | Single-turn request and response | Multi-turn agent trajectories across tools, memory, and environments |
| Primary Failure Mode | Persona drift, ungrounded speculation | Context rot, distraction by verbose logs, stale document conflicts |
| Primary Tooling | System prompt templates, prompt playground UI | Vector databases, graph RAG, compaction APIs, tool observation filters |

## Where I would push back on the hype

Context engineering is now getting its own hype cycle, and the pattern from the prompt era is repeating, so it is worth being clear about limits. Better context does not fix a model that lacks the underlying capability for a task. It does not substitute for evals, and teams that tune context without a measurement loop are just generating vibes with extra steps. And there is a real ceiling on how much curation effort makes sense for low-stakes use cases. A casual chat interface does not need the context discipline of an agent that touches production systems.

But for anything agentic, anything long-running, anything where the model acts rather than just answers, I would put context design at the center of the build. The prompt is one input among many, and usually not the one that decides whether the thing works. The window is the product. What you let into it is the job.


If retrieval is the part you are trying to place inside that architecture, [Is RAG Dead?](/writing/is-rag-dead-2026) is my answer to what long context and agentic search actually changed. If the system is already running and the question is whether a context change helped, [Evals Are the New Test Suite](/writing/evals-are-the-new-test-suite) is the measurement layer I would add next. My [Frontier Models](/frontier-models) tracker lists the context window and price for each current model.

### Moving to Biweekly Releases by Treating QA as a Reusable System

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/qa-automation-daily-deploys
- Published: 2026-04-29
- Topic: Quality Engineering
- Excerpt: I designed an automation framework and release workflow that turned manual validation work into reusable infrastructure. The lesson was that stable narrow coverage beats broad flaky coverage almost every time.

Most teams who say they want to ship more often are really saying they want the confidence to ship more often. The deploy pipeline is rarely the thing that breaks. The thing that breaks is the validation work in front of it, which gets slower as the product gets larger until "ship" becomes a multi-day decision instead of a single push.

That was the situation when I started this work. Manual testing across multiple tech stacks was slowing releases and letting defects reach production after long, repetitive validation cycles. The team did not need a faster pipeline. They needed a way to trust the pipeline they already had.

## The Real Problem Was Trust, Not Coverage

Three pain points kept showing up. Release validation took too long and blocked deployment momentum. Coverage gaps made recurring production defects difficult to prevent. And QA work was too dependent on manual repetition instead of reusable test assets, which meant every cycle started over from scratch.

Slow validation was costing the team speed. Escaped defects were eroding confidence in each release. The combination is a particularly painful kind of operational debt because it makes everyone look like they are working hard while the product still feels brittle. The fix had to make validation faster and the underlying product more trustworthy at the same time.

## What The Framework Actually Did

The instinct most teams reach for first is to add more tests. That is the wrong instinct. Brittle test inventory does not build confidence. It builds backlog.

The framework I built focused on stable critical-path automation before anything else. I identified high-value regression paths, implemented reusable test components and page objects so the suite could be maintained, and integrated the automation into CI so failures surfaced before release handoff instead of during it.

Two principles ended up shaping the rest of the work. Reliability and maintainability mattered more than chasing the largest possible test count. And reporting needed to group failures by likely cause instead of raw failure volume, because a wall of red is operationally identical to no signal at all.

The suite ran on Cypress for end-to-end tests, Postman for API tests, and JMeter for load tests, and it grew to more than 400 manual and automated tests across two products.

## What Changed

Releases moved from monthly to biweekly, and release validation time dropped 30%. Alongside the new deployment rules I set with engineering and DevOps, critical defects dropped 90%.

The harder-to-measure outcome was that QA work stopped being the bottleneck conversation. The team could plan releases around real signal instead of around how nervous someone was about a particular release. That kind of confidence does not show up in a single metric, but it changes how the team operates day to day.

## What I Would Bring Forward

Stable tests beat broad flaky coverage every time. Anyone who has had to triage a flaky suite during a release weekend already knows this, but it is worth saying out loud because the temptation in test strategy is always to add more, and the better move is usually to remove the unstable parts and double down on the reliable ones.

Automation adoption depends as much on documentation and training as on the framework itself. A great suite that nobody understands is a single-owner suite, and single-owner systems do not survive turnover.

If you want the broader frame on quality work in production, [Building Reliable Software Systems](/writing/building-reliable-software-systems) is the long-form thesis, and [Launching RunningMate by Treating Quality as Product Definition](/writing/runningmate-platform-launch) is where the same instincts run inside a launch instead of a release loop.

### Preventing Outages by Tying Performance Monitoring to User Workflows

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/proactive-performance-intelligence
- Published: 2026-04-29
- Topic: Reliability
- Excerpt: I built a performance intelligence workflow that connected monitoring, load testing, and incident review into a single loop. The shift was framing performance work around user impact instead of raw infrastructure metrics.

The problem with most performance dashboards is that they are tuned for the wrong audience. They are built for the people who set them up, not the people who have to act on them. So infrastructure metrics scroll past, alerts fire on noise, and the only signal anyone actually trusts is a customer ticket. By that point, the team is in incident response mode, and incident response is a worse place to do reliability work than planning is.

That was the starting state when I took on this work. The team was reacting to performance issues after user impact, and the existing monitoring did not connect technical signals to product risk clearly enough. Alerts were either too noisy or too late to guide action. Performance regressions were difficult to connect to specific releases. And stakeholders lacked a clear view of which reliability issues mattered most, which made it hard to prioritize work outside of an outage.

Every preventable outage or slow workflow was weakening user trust and pulling the team away from planned product work. Reliability had become an interrupt loop instead of a planning input.

## The Reframe

The shift was to treat performance as something measured in user workflows, not in infrastructure metrics in isolation. A CPU spike does not matter on its own. A CPU spike that correlates with a slow voter outreach workflow during peak traffic absolutely matters. The same is true in reverse. A long tail latency in an unused endpoint can sit on a dashboard for months without doing harm.

I connected monitoring, load testing, and incident review into a single workflow. Performance thresholds got defined around user-facing workflows so the alerting was telling the team something about the customer experience, not about the back end. Dashboards separated actionable signals from background noise, which sounds simple and is operationally hard. Load testing and incident review loops caught recurring bottlenecks before they became outages.

The principles ended up being clear. Set alert thresholds around user impact instead of raw infrastructure noise. Track regressions by product workflow so fixes can be prioritized against the parts of the product that matter most. Use incident reviews to update monitoring coverage instead of just documenting failures. The last one was the most important. An incident that does not improve the monitoring system is a missed opportunity, even if the immediate fix lands.

## What Changed

Uptime reached 99.999%, and more issues were caught before users felt them. Performance reporting became part of regular product review instead of an artifact of incident response.

The cultural change was the harder thing to measure. Performance tradeoffs started showing up in planning conversations. Engineers could point at a workflow and say "this is going to start hurting at scale" with evidence behind the claim. Stakeholders could see which reliability investments would pay off in customer experience. The team stopped arguing about whether to do the work and started arguing about which slice of the work was worth doing first.

## What I Would Bring Forward

Monitoring is only useful when it changes what the team does next. A dashboard nobody acts on is a screensaver. Performance work lands better when it is framed around user workflows, not isolated infrastructure metrics, because that framing is the one that makes tradeoffs legible to non-engineers.

The other thing I would change next time is pairing the dashboards with runbooks earlier. Each alert needed a clearer owner and a clearer first-response path, and that part of the system would have made the early days of the rollout less ambiguous than it ended up being.

If you want the broader thesis, [Building Reliable Software Systems](/writing/building-reliable-software-systems) is the long-form companion, and [Keeping a Civic Engagement Platform Reliable While It Reached 60M+ Voters](/writing/scaling-civic-engagement-platform) is the same set of instincts applied to scale instead of to monitoring directly.

### Keeping a Civic Engagement Platform Reliable While It Reached 60M+ Voters

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/scaling-civic-engagement-platform
- Published: 2026-04-29
- Topic: Reliability
- Excerpt: I led quality and reliability work for a civic engagement platform that campaigns used to reach more than 60 million unique voters in 2024. The constraint that shaped everything was that election deadlines do not move, so the work had to hold up without giving back release speed.

Election software has fixed deadlines and uneven traffic. Most product reliability stories let you choose between scaling carefully and shipping quickly. In civic tech, the calendar takes that choice off the table. The platform has to grow, the new features have to land, and the cycle still ends on a specific Tuesday in November regardless of what shape the product is in.

I led quality and reliability work for a civic engagement platform through the 2024 election cycle, when campaigns used it to reach more than 60 million unique voters. The job was to keep the team's confidence in releases high enough that the size of that audience never felt like a reason to slow down.

## What Was Really At Stake

Reliability issues during election periods do something specific. They damage client trust at the same moment voter outreach is supposed to be working. A platform that fails on the last Saturday before an election does not get a chance to apologize.

The pressure on the team showed up in three places. Manual test coverage could not keep up with rapid feature development. Critical user paths needed stronger protection before election-day traffic. And release cycles had to get faster without lowering confidence, because slowing down would have meant fewer of the customer-facing improvements campaign teams were depending on.

## How The Strategy Got Built

The first move was to map the highest-risk voter outreach workflows and platform edge cases honestly. Not the full surface, just the parts where a failure during peak traffic would actually break a customer's day. That mapping shaped where automation went first and where manual review was still worth the time.

I then expanded automated coverage across those critical product paths and created release reporting that made readiness and risk easier for stakeholders to inspect. The goal of the reporting was not status updates. It was making a release decision easier to make. If a stakeholder could not look at the dashboard and understand whether to ship, the dashboard was not doing its job.

Two principles ended up guiding the rest of the work. First, prioritize critical election-day flows before lower-risk coverage expansion. Broad shallow coverage feels like progress, but it does not protect the workflows that actually matter when the cycle peaks. Second, focus reporting on signals that could change a release decision. Anything else is decoration.

## What Changed

Campaigns used the platform to reach more than 60 million unique voters in 2024. Over my three years as the team's QA analyst, across the two products I covered, uptime held at 99.999%, critical defects dropped 90%, and release efficiency improved 50%, which came from new deployment rules and more than 400 manual and automated tests.

The deeper change was operational. The team stopped arguing about whether a release was safe and started arguing about which of the remaining tradeoffs was worth making. That is a much healthier place for a release conversation to live, and it is the version of the team that survived peak election traffic without a major incident.

## What I Would Bring Forward

High-scale reliability work has to start with the workflows users cannot afford to lose. There is always a temptation to chase coverage breadth or vanity metrics, especially under pressure, because it feels productive. The teams that hold up under real load are the ones who knew, ahead of time, which two or three workflows were the entire game.

A faster release process only works when confidence signals are visible and trusted. If the team has to debate the meaning of every metric, the metrics are not the bottleneck. The visibility is.

If you want the broader thesis on reliability across systems work, [Building Reliable Software Systems](/writing/building-reliable-software-systems) goes deeper, and [Preventing Outages by Tying Performance Monitoring to User Workflows](/writing/proactive-performance-intelligence) is the companion case study on the monitoring side.

### Owning a Peer-to-Peer Texting Platform When Campaign Calendars Don't Move

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/textout-platform
- Published: 2026-04-29
- Topic: Product Strategy
- Excerpt: I owned product vision for a peer-to-peer texting platform built for campaigns. Here's what I learned about treating onboarding speed and dashboard clarity as the product, not the surrounding work.

Most campaign software gets judged on one question. Can a team go from a signed contract to active outreach before the calendar runs out? That sounds obvious, but it changes how you have to think about a peer-to-peer texting product. The deadline is fixed by an election, not by a roadmap. If onboarding takes a week, that is one less week of voter contact, and a campaign manager will remember that long after the cycle ends.

I owned product vision for a peer-to-peer texting platform built for that environment. The job was to connect what campaign managers actually needed during launch with the engineering work that would make the product easier to adopt under pressure.

## The Problem Was Not Features, It Was Time-To-Useful

Campaign teams already understood texting. They did not need to be sold on the channel. What they needed was a platform that did not punish them for being new to it. The pain showed up in three places. Onboarding required manual configuration and repeated technical handoffs. Campaign managers had limited visibility into message performance and volunteer activity once they were live. And training new users was too slow for teams operating against fixed election timelines.

In campaign software, slow onboarding and unclear performance data are not rough edges. They cost teams the days when voter contact matters most. That framing mattered because it pushed the team to treat setup and reporting as core product, not as wraparound services.

## Where I Pointed The Roadmap

I started with research instead of feature requests. Interviews with campaign managers and active users showed that the friction was concentrated in the first few sessions and in the recurring reporting loop. Once a user was past launch and had a working dashboard, the workflow was fine. The product was losing trust at the front door.

That changed prioritization. Dashboard clarity and onboarding speed moved ahead of newer feature ideas, even when those features were louder in stakeholder conversations. I translated research findings into user stories with acceptance criteria so the engineering work tracked back to specific moments where users had been struggling.

The other shift was treating automation as a product feature, not as an internal optimization. The GCP-backed setup work that reduced manual configuration was visible to the customer because it changed the calendar. A faster path from contract to first usable workflow was, by itself, a product value proposition.

## What Changed

Engagement lifted by 35%, and dashboard improvements gave campaign managers clearer visibility into message delivery, volunteer activity, and outreach performance, which made it easier for them to act on the data instead of asking us for it.

The numbers mattered, but the underlying shift mattered more. The product stopped feeling like infrastructure that needed a specialist and started feeling like a tool a campaign manager could pick up and run.

## What I Would Bring Forward

The strongest lesson from this work was that automation creates more product value when it removes visible user friction, not just internal effort. Internal automation that no customer ever sees is fine, but it does not change the product story. Automation that turns "we need to set this up for you" into "you can do this yourself this afternoon" changes the conversation about what the product is.

The other lesson was about deadlines as a design constraint. Campaign software has to respect calendar pressure because users do not get to move the deadline. That constraint forced sharper prioritization than most B2B SaaS contexts allow, and the parts of that discipline I would carry into any product where the customer is racing the clock. If a feature does not help in the first week, it usually should not be the next thing built.

If you want the longer view of how I think about reliability and quality in product work, [Building Reliable Software Systems](/writing/building-reliable-software-systems) is the closest companion piece, and [Launching RunningMate by Treating Quality as Product Definition](/writing/runningmate-platform-launch) is the next case study where the same prioritization instincts had to scale across more functions.

### Interchange IQ: Building a Payment Fee Analyzer Around Real Processor Economics

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/interchange-iq-payment-fee-analyzer
- Published: 2026-04-02
- Topic: Payments
- Excerpt: I built Interchange IQ to make payment processor comparisons actually legible. It models flat-rate vs. interchange-plus pricing using published interchange data, card mix, and breakeven logic.

If you want to use the tool first, open [Interchange IQ](/fintech-tools/interchange-iq).

Most merchants know they are paying for card processing. Far fewer know what they are actually paying for.

That confusion is not accidental. Processor pricing is full of blended rates, flat-rate convenience, card-mix variation, scheme complexity, and enterprise plans that only become legible once a business is already large enough to negotiate. For operators trying to make a clean decision, the market often feels deliberately hard to compare.

I built Interchange IQ to make that comparison more concrete. The product is designed to answer a practical question. Given your monthly volume, average ticket size, and card mix, how different do processor economics actually look?

## The Problem

For many businesses, processor choice is treated as a branding or convenience decision when it is really a margin decision. The challenge is that the headline price rarely tells the whole story. Flat-rate pricing is easy to understand but can hide meaningful overpayment at scale. Interchange-plus pricing can be cheaper, but it is harder to reason about without the underlying rate structure. Ticket size changes the impact of fixed per-transaction fees, and a debit-heavy business does not behave the same way economically as an Amex-heavy one.

A merchant does not need a theory lecture on payments. They need a model they can manipulate.

## Why The Tool Starts With Published Interchange Data

The core product decision was to make the calculator legible from first principles. Interchange IQ uses representative published interchange values and public processor pricing assumptions to show where the costs actually come from. That matters because a comparison tool is much more useful when you can see the difference between network economics, processor markup, volume sensitivity, and ticket-size sensitivity in the same view.

This keeps the product grounded in real payments structure instead of turning it into a black-box recommendation engine. It does not try to predict every custom contract. It gives you a way to understand the shape of the decision and the conditions that change it.

## The Key Product Decisions

Card mix is where processor comparisons start to become real. A business with a heavy debit profile behaves very differently from one with a premium credit and Amex-heavy mix. Showing only a headline rate would flatten that difference and make the tool less honest. That is why Interchange IQ lets you adjust monthly processing volume, average transaction size, credit-card share, and Amex share within the credit mix. Those inputs turn the product from a static comparison table into a working model.

I also wanted to compare flat-rate and interchange-plus on the same surface rather than implicitly arguing for one before showing the math. Interchange IQ places both options side by side so you can see when simplicity is worth paying for and when it becomes too expensive. A smaller operator may decide flat rate is still the right answer. A larger operator may realize the markup on interchange-plus becomes compelling once volume rises or average ticket size increases.

The cheapest option at one ticket size is not necessarily the cheapest option at another, which is why the tool includes breakeven logic. A single "best processor" label is too shallow. The better question is at what point does the economic logic flip. Breakeven analysis teaches you how the market works, not just what the calculator currently outputs. For how I think about pricing as product work more broadly, see [Treating Pricing as Product Work, Not a Finance-Only Exercise](/writing/pricing-strategy-initiative).

## How The Experience Works

The interface is intentionally direct. Inputs define the business profile. Summary stats show the cheapest current option and monthly fee impact. A ranked comparison table surfaces effective rates and fee outcomes. And explanatory copy clarifies what card mix and pricing models actually mean, because payments products can become abstract very quickly. The structure keeps you oriented around real operating questions. What happens if my volume doubles, what happens if my average ticket falls, how much is flat-rate convenience costing me, when does interchange-plus start to win.

## Tradeoffs I Chose On Purpose

I made a deliberate call to cover major processors and representative rate assumptions rather than model every private contract or every network nuance. That keeps the experience readable and useful for decision framing without trying to be exhaustive. I also chose to show the math drivers instead of dressing them up as a mysterious score, because in payments a product builds more trust when users can understand the model underneath it. And I included explanations for why debit, credit, and Amex matter differently, because a calculator without explanation only helps people who already know the answer.

## What This Project Taught Me

Payments is a strong product-design domain because so much of the value comes from making complexity legible. The most important lesson here was that comparison products work best when they help users build intuition, not just produce outputs. The breakeven model, the card-mix controls, and the flat-rate versus interchange-plus framing all push in that direction.

I came away with a more durable belief about fintech products: users do not always need every edge case modeled. They need enough structure to see how the economics behave and enough clarity to make a better decision than they would have made with marketing pages alone.

## Try The Live Product

You can run your own scenarios in [Interchange IQ](/fintech-tools/interchange-iq). The fastest way to understand the product is to keep volume constant, then move average ticket size and card mix around. That exposes how quickly processor economics change once you stop treating the headline rate as the whole story.

If you want the adjacent reads, [Building an Investment Research Platform That Prefers Clarity Over Spreadsheet Sprawl](/writing/building-an-investment-research-platform) is the other product essay where I am trying to make a financial workflow easier to inspect, and [Reasoning Model Economics: When Opus Is Worth It and When Sonnet Does the Job](/writing/reasoning-model-economics-when-to-use-which) is the same basic argument about clearer tradeoffs, just applied to model cost instead of processor pricing.

### Building an Investment Research Platform That Prefers Clarity Over Spreadsheet Sprawl

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/building-an-investment-research-platform
- Published: 2026-04-02
- Topic: Fintech Product
- Excerpt: I built an investment research workspace because my own research workflow was scattered across too many tabs. Here's what I decided to include, what I left out, and why.

If you want to see the product before reading the breakdown, open the [Investment Research Platform](/investments).

Most personal investing workflows break down in the same place, which is that the analysis is scattered. Price charts live in one tab, financial statements in another, notes in a spreadsheet, and portfolio tracking in a tool that has no idea why you bought the stock in the first place. I built this project because I wanted a research workflow that felt more like a decision workspace than a collection of disconnected utilities. The goal was not to recreate a full institutional terminal. The goal was to make the most important parts of equity research easier to review, compare, and revisit without adding more friction.

## The Problem This Product Tries To Solve

Retail research tools often force a tradeoff between breadth and clarity. Broad platforms surface a huge number of metrics, but they bury the signal under dense tables and too many navigation layers. Simpler trackers make portfolio monitoring easy, but they stop short of helping you understand the business behind the position. Spreadsheet-based workflows are flexible, but they are tedious to maintain and hard to keep consistent over time.

That combination creates a quiet failure mode, which is that you can gather plenty of information without actually improving the decision. I wanted a workspace that answered three practical questions quickly. What does this company look like right now, how does the valuation compare with the operating profile, and what does this mean for the positions I already hold?

## Why The Product Uses Curated Snapshots

One of the earliest product decisions was to avoid pretending this needed to be a tick-by-tick trading terminal. The platform is built around curated company snapshots, valuation panels, price history, and financial statement views. That structure matters because the highest-value research questions usually do not require every possible data point in real time. They require trustworthy context with clear fallbacks.

That is why the product leans on a curated symbol set and snapshot-backed research rather than an unlimited search surface. It narrows the scope enough to keep the experience reliable while still giving the user a strong research loop. The research experience is more stable because every symbol can be shaped into the same interface, the UI can emphasize interpretation instead of raw data dumping, and the system can degrade more gracefully when a data source is incomplete. In other words, curation is not a limitation here. It is part of the product strategy.

## The Core Product Decisions

The route is organized around two tabs: research and portfolio. That sounds simple, but it changes the product meaningfully. Instead of treating research as a separate activity from portfolio management, the platform lets both workflows share the same mental model. You can move from a holding to a deeper review of the underlying company without changing tools or losing context. That matters because investing decisions are rarely isolated. The useful question is not just "Is this stock interesting?" It is "Is this stock interesting relative to what I already own?"

I chose browser-local persistence for portfolio tracking instead of building a full account system. For this project, that was the right call. The value of the portfolio tab is fast iteration, not multi-user infrastructure. Local persistence keeps the workflow immediate and private, removes sign-in friction, and lets the product behave more like a personal research notebook than a brokerage dashboard. Adding authentication would have made the product feel more complete on paper, but it would not have made the core research loop materially better.

A ratio by itself rarely helps. A low multiple can signal value, but it can also reflect deteriorating fundamentals. A premium multiple may be justified if growth, margins, and balance-sheet quality support it. That is why the experience is organized around adjacent panels instead of isolated numbers. The user can move across valuation, growth, profitability, financial statements, industry context, and price history without reorienting every time. If a metric invites interpretation, the supporting context should be close by.

## Tradeoffs I Would Make Again

A smaller but cleaner research universe is better than a giant index with uneven quality. The product is intentionally framed as a workspace, not a brokerage clone, and that keeps the experience centered on research and portfolio understanding instead of trying to imitate execution platforms. There are plenty of finance products that use metric density as a stand-in for usefulness. I would rather show fewer things, arranged with more intent, than turn the page into a wall of numbers that looks impressive but slows down judgment.

Building finance products is often an exercise in restraint. The temptation is to add more coverage, more models, more feeds, and more technical sophistication. But most of the user value comes from making it easier to move from raw information to a coherent point of view. This project reinforced a product lesson I trust across domains, which is that good tools reduce decision fatigue before they add decision power.

## Try The Live Product

You can explore the full product at [Investment Research Platform](/investments). The quickest way to understand the experience is to move between the research and portfolio views and notice how the product keeps analysis and position management in the same frame. That integration is the point of the project.

If you want the adjacent reads, [Interchange IQ: Building a Payment Fee Analyzer Around Real Processor Economics](/writing/interchange-iq-payment-fee-analyzer) is the other product breakdown where I am trying to make dense financial logic legible, and [Reasoning Model Economics: When Opus Is Worth It and When Sonnet Does the Job](/writing/reasoning-model-economics-when-to-use-which) gets at the same idea from the AI-tooling side of decision support.
