### Treating Pricing as Product Work, Not a Finance-Only Exercise

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/pricing-strategy-initiative
- Published: 2026-04-29
- Topic: Pricing Strategy
- Excerpt: I led a cross-functional pricing initiative that connected market analysis, product value, and financial modeling into a clearer pricing strategy. The shift was treating pricing as a product decision, not a spreadsheet exercise.

Most pricing decisions get made on the wrong side of the building. Finance owns the model, sales owns the negotiation, and product gets pulled in at the end to validate that the packaging story is coherent. By that point the structure is already locked, and product's role becomes either rubber-stamping a deck or arguing for changes that finance has to redo from scratch.

That model produces pricing that captures a fraction of the product's actual value. The right framing is the opposite. Pricing is a product decision that carries financial implications, not a financial decision that carries product implications. When I led this initiative, that was the real shift. Everything else followed from it.

## What The Org Was Actually Stuck On

The organization needed a pricing strategy that reflected product value, market position, and customer willingness to pay rather than inherited assumptions from earlier in the company's life. Three frictions kept showing up. Pricing conversations were split across sales, finance, product, and engineering, with no shared model anyone could reason from. Decision-makers lacked a shared view of product value and market comparison, which meant every meeting started over from first principles. And packaging decisions needed clearer revenue and customer-impact tradeoffs before they could be made with confidence.

Weak pricing strategy leaves revenue on the table while making future packaging changes harder to explain to customers. The cost is not just immediate. It compounds, because each pricing change you cannot defend cleanly trains the customer base to negotiate harder on the next one.

## How The Work Got Structured

The first task was to build the analytical and stakeholder alignment layer that would let pricing become a product decision instead of a finance-only exercise. That meant researching market benchmarks and competitor packaging seriously, not just collecting screenshots of pricing pages. It meant modeling pricing scenarios against revenue, adoption, and operational constraints with enough rigor that the model could survive cross-functional pressure. And it meant creating executive-facing materials that made tradeoffs explicit, not buried inside a recommended option.

The principles that ended up driving the strategy were direct. Center the work on product value and customer segment fit, not on what the existing price card happened to say. Separate near-term revenue opportunities from longer-term packaging bets so each was being argued on the right time horizon. And make the underlying model reusable so the work could guide future product lines without being recreated each time.

The cross-functional alignment was the part that moved the recommendation from a recommendation into an actual decision. Engineering, sales, finance, and leadership all had to be able to see their own assumptions inside the model. That is what turned individual objections into shared questions about which scenario to pick.

## What Changed

The initiative generated $4M in additional revenue in 2024. The market analysis framework got adopted for future pricing work, which is a more durable outcome than the immediate revenue lift. Executive buy-in came through clear scenario modeling rather than through a single recommended price, which made the resulting decision much easier to defend internally and externally.

## What I Would Bring Forward

Pricing work is product work when it changes packaging, value communication, and roadmap tradeoffs. Treating it as anything else leaves money on the table and creates packaging decisions that the product team has to live with for years.

Stakeholder alignment improves when every group can see its own assumptions reflected in the model. The temptation in pricing work is to hide the assumptions inside a confident recommendation, because it feels cleaner. The cleaner version is also the version that falls apart the first time a single assumption gets challenged. Showing the model openly is the shorter path to a real decision.

The thing I would do differently next time is add customer validation earlier, so willingness-to-pay evidence sits beside the market and financial analysis from the start instead of arriving late as a sanity check.

For more on building products around financial decisions specifically, [Building an Investment Research Platform That Prefers Clarity Over Spreadsheet Sprawl](/writing/building-an-investment-research-platform) is the closest companion piece, and [Interchange IQ: Building a Payment Fee Analyzer Around Real Processor Economics](/writing/interchange-iq-payment-fee-analyzer) is the version where pricing logic is the product itself.

---


### Building the Pulse Dashboards as One Product System, Not Nine Pages

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/building-the-pulse-dashboard-family
- Published: 2026-06-16
- Topic: Product Design
- Excerpt: I built the Pulse dashboards as a single product family with a shared interaction model and domain-specific framing, so each new surface is faster to ship and easier to learn.

If you want to see the family before reading the breakdown, the [portfolio](/portfolio) lists the full set of live dashboards.

At some point I stopped building individual dashboards and started building a system that happens to render as many dashboards. The Pulse family spans sports, media, developer trends, and politics, and from the outside each surface looks bespoke to its domain. The [NFL](/nfl) page knows about weeks and conferences, the [earthquake](/earthquake-pulse) page knows about magnitude and regions, the [Bay Area transit](/bay-area-transit) page knows about lines and departure boards. Underneath, though, they are the same product. I made that choice early, and it is the reason a new dashboard now takes days instead of weeks, and the reason someone who has used one of them already knows how to use the next.

## One Interaction Model, Many Domains

The shared spine is an interaction model, not a template. Every Pulse dashboard opens on a compact first screen that surfaces pressure and movement before anything else, so the first thing you see is what changed and what is under tension rather than a wall of tables. Every one uses the same deep-linkable URL state, so a view and a selected entity live in the address bar and a link drops someone exactly where you were. They share snapshot handling and a common card and component layer, which is why the [MLB](/mlb), [NBA](/nba), and [Premier League](/premier-league) surfaces feel like cousins even though their data could not be more different. The bet I was making is that a learnable family beats a collection of clever one-offs. Once you understand how to read movement on the [La Liga](/la-liga) page, you understand the [World Cup](/world-cup-2026) page and the [polling aggregator](/polling-aggregator) without relearning anything, and that transfer is worth more than the novelty of designing each from scratch. Designing every dashboard fresh would have produced more variety and a slower, more confusing product. The shared model keeps the family coherent while the domain framing preserves what is genuinely unique to each subject.

## The Architecture Underneath

The reason the interaction model holds across so many surfaces is that the data architecture is one repeated pattern. Each dashboard starts from a committed snapshot, which a builder script regenerates, which a scheduled GitHub Action runs on a cadence that fits the domain, which accessors read, which a thin read API exposes to the page. That pattern now backs more than fifteen dashboards, and its uniformity is the point. When the shape of the data pipeline is identical from [Formula 1](/formula-1) to [golf](/golf) to [GitHub trending](/github-trending-pulse), adding a new surface is mostly a question of writing the builder and the domain framing, because everything downstream already exists. The sameness is not laziness. It is leverage, and it is the difference between a system and a pile of pages.

## The Tradeoffs I Made on Purpose

Two tradeoffs defined the family, and I would make both again. The first is snapshot-backed data over fully live runtime dependencies. These products are read far more than they are transacted on, so second-by-second freshness matters less than predictable performance and operational durability. A snapshot that refreshes on a sensible schedule will never melt down because an upstream API rate-limited me mid-render, and that reliability is worth more to a reader checking the [news pulse](/news-pulse) than a live feed that occasionally fails in their face. The second tradeoff is editorial framing over raw data density. It is tempting to dump every available table and call it thorough, but a good dashboard leads with pressure, movement, and the question the reader is most likely to ask first, and lets the depth sit one layer down for the people who want it. Density feels impressive and reads exhausting. Choosing what to surface first is the actual design work, and it is what separates a dashboard you understand in seconds from one you have to excavate.

## The North Star and the Honest Gap

The metric I kept returning to is time to useful context, the gap between landing on a dashboard and understanding what changed and why it matters. Every decision in the family bends toward shrinking that gap, from the compact first screen to the shared interaction grammar that means you are never learning a new product from zero. That is the thing I am proudest of, and it is also where I want to be honest about what is still missing. The common product logic is strong, but the family is still discovered route by route. There is no shared landing hub that presents the Pulse dashboards as the single system they actually are, so someone who finds the transit page has no obvious path to the rest of them. The product system is real on the inside and invisible on the outside, and closing that gap with a proper hub is the work I have not finished. A system the user cannot see as a system is only doing half its job.

The fastest way to understand the family right now is to open two siblings back to back, say the [NFL](/nfl) dashboard and the [earthquake pulse](/earthquake-pulse), and notice how quickly the second one feels familiar even though the subject is completely different. That recognition is the whole product. If you want the deeper builds, [Building News Pulse to Compare How Major Outlets Cover the Same Story](/writing/building-news-pulse-dashboard) and [Building a World Cup Dashboard](/writing/building-a-world-cup-dashboard) each go one level into a single member of the family.

---


### Building News Pulse to Compare How Major Outlets Cover the Same Story

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/building-news-pulse-dashboard
- Published: 2026-04-02
- Topic: Media Analytics
- Excerpt: I built News Pulse because it's surprisingly tedious to compare coverage across outlets in a structured way. Here's the product thinking behind the RSS foundation, the analysis layer, and the deliberate tradeoffs.

If you want to explore the product before reading the breakdown, open [News Pulse Dashboard](/news-pulse).

Reading one publication tells you what happened. Reading several publications tells you how the story is being framed. The gap between those two things is where News Pulse lives.

I built this project because it is surprisingly tedious to compare coverage across outlets in a structured way. Opening a half-dozen homepages gives you raw exposure, but not much synthesis. You can feel the differences in framing, frequency, and tone, but it takes effort to turn that into something legible. The goal of News Pulse was to make that comparison easier without overengineering the stack.

## The Problem Behind The Product

People who follow the news closely often want to answer questions that consumer news products are not really designed to answer. They want to know which outlets are covering a story heavily right now, whether the headlines are converging on the same terms or splitting into different frames, whether the tone is mostly urgent or negative or neutral, and how fast a theme spreads across sources. Most consumer news products are designed to deliver articles, not help people analyze editorial patterns. Enterprise media intelligence tools exist, but they are often heavier and more specialized than what this use case needs. That left a good product gap, a lightweight dashboard for comparing how several major outlets are talking about the same news cycle.

## Why RSS Was The Right Foundation

The product starts with RSS because RSS is still one of the cleanest ways to capture headline-level editorial output across publishers. That choice shaped the entire build. It kept the data model focused on headlines and feed metadata, avoided a much more fragile scraping workflow, and made update timing easier to reason about. It also allowed the product to stay legible as a portfolio project instead of turning into an infrastructure project. RSS is not glamorous, but it is reliable enough for this problem. That is often the right product decision.

## The Core Decisions And Tradeoffs

News Pulse is not trying to be another article reader. It is organized around three higher-level views (headlines, coverage, and analysis) because the value of the product is comparative, not archival. The user should feel like they are seeing patterns across sources rather than just skimming a merged list of links.

One of the most deliberate choices in the product was to keep the analysis layer lightweight. The dashboard extracts topics, summarizes source behavior, and performs headline-level sentiment without introducing a large external dependency chain. Headlines are short and structured enough for lightweight heuristics to be useful, the goal is directional media intelligence rather than perfect semantic classification, and keeping the stack lighter makes the product easier to maintain and reason about. This is a case where "good enough and understandable" is better than "technically impressive but hard to trust."

Live feeds are messy. Publishers change formats, feeds fail, and partial outages happen. The product handles that reality by surfacing feed errors without collapsing the whole experience. If one source is unavailable, the dashboard should still tell the truth about what it can show rather than fail silently or imply complete coverage. That is a small but important product choice.

## Why A Dependency-Light Stack Was Worth Protecting

There is always pressure to make media-analysis products feel more "AI-native" than they need to be. This project pushed me in the opposite direction. I wanted the product to feel sharp, timely, and interpretable without becoming dependent on a chain of external services that would add cost, complexity, and brittleness. For this use case, a lighter stack offered real advantages: faster iteration, clearer system behavior, easier debugging, and a tighter connection between the visible output and the underlying logic. That tradeoff made the project more useful as a product surface and more durable as a codebase.

## What This Project Taught Me

News products become more interesting when they move one step up the abstraction ladder. A feed is useful. A comparative view of editorial patterns is often more useful. This project reinforced a product principle I keep coming back to, which is that if users are already doing synthesis manually, there is probably room to build a better intermediate layer. In this case, that layer is not a full newsroom platform. It is a clean dashboard that makes coverage differences easier to spot. It also reminded me that "lightweight" is not the same as "thin." A product can do meaningful analytical work without pretending every problem requires a giant model stack.

## Try The Live Product

You can explore the full experience at [News Pulse Dashboard](/news-pulse). The easiest way to understand the product is to start on headlines, pick a source, then switch back to the all-sources coverage and analysis views. That transition shows the core point of the project, which is turning separate feeds into a clearer picture of the news cycle.

---


### Building a GitHub Trending Dashboard That Is Not Just a Leaderboard

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/building-a-github-trending-dashboard
- Published: 2026-06-11
- Topic: Developer Tools
- Excerpt: I built GitHub Trending Pulse to turn GitHub Search data into a daily snapshot across languages, topics, and weekly star movement, instead of treating trending as a static list.

If you want to see the product before reading the breakdown, open [GitHub Trending Pulse](/github-trending-pulse).

Everyone who writes code keeps a loose mental list of what is happening in open source, and almost nobody has a good way to maintain it. GitHub itself has a trending page, but it is a single ranked list that resets every day, and a list is a strange way to understand momentum. What I actually want to know is not which repository has the most stars, because the answer to that has been the same set of giant projects for years. I want to know what is moving, in which language, around which topic, and whether it is accelerating or already cooling off. So I built GitHub Trending Pulse to treat trending as a shape rather than a leaderboard.

## Discovery on GitHub is noisier than it should be

The frustrating thing about finding interesting projects on GitHub is that the relevant signals all live in different places. The genuinely popular projects sit at the top of any all-time star search and rarely move, the freshly active repositories are buried under that weight, and topic-specific momentum, the stuff happening right now in one niche, requires a search query you have to construct by hand. None of those three views talk to each other, so building an accurate picture of what is happening means running several searches and holding the results in your head. That is a lot of effort to answer a question I ask almost every week.

So the dashboard does the organizing instead of the reader. It pulls from the public GitHub Search API and arranges the results into fourteen segments split across languages and topics, so the page is not one list but a set of focused windows into different corners of the ecosystem. Looking at what is active in a specific language is a different question from looking at what is active around a specific topic, and the segmented layout lets you ask either one without writing a query. The value is in the curation of those windows, not in reprinting a single ranking that anyone could already find.

## Why it shows movement, not totals

This is the decision that makes the product different from the official trending page, and it is the one I care most about. A single daily list can only ever show you a state, which is who is on top today. It cannot show you change, because it has no memory of yesterday. GitHub Trending Pulse carries weekly star deltas forward across days, so each repository shows how its stars have moved over the trailing week, not just its all-time count. That difference sounds small and is actually the whole thesis. An all-time star count tells you what was popular at some point in history. A weekly delta tells you what is gaining attention right now, and a delta tracked across several days tells you whether that attention is accelerating or fading.

Acceleration is the signal that genuinely useful discovery is built on, and it is exactly the thing a snapshot with no history cannot give you. A project that added a few thousand stars this week is a different story from one that has been quietly adding the same number every week for a year, and you can only tell those apart if the data remembers. By carrying the deltas forward, the dashboard turns a flat ranking into something closer to a velocity reading, which is what I actually wanted from a trending tool in the first place.

## The snapshot that makes the memory possible

The dashboard reads from a snapshot committed to the repository as a plain TypeScript file, generated by a build script that queries the GitHub Search API, shapes the fourteen segments, and writes the file. A scheduled job refreshes it daily, and the running site never calls GitHub at request time. The snapshot pattern is not just about reliability here, although it gives me that too, with instant page loads and no risk of hitting an API rate limit while someone is reading. It is what makes the weekly movement possible at all. Because each refresh commits a dated snapshot, the data has a history, and that history is precisely what lets the dashboard show deltas instead of a stateless ranking. A live API call at request time would only ever know about right now. A committed daily snapshot knows about the trend.

The refresh follows the same conservative rule as the rest of the family, so a failed or empty fetch keeps the previous snapshot rather than wiping good data, which means a bad GitHub response cannot blank the board. For a developer who pops in once a week to see what is new, the worst outcome would be an empty page, so the pipeline always prefers the last good snapshot over nothing.

## What I took away from it

The thing this project clarified for me is that a leaderboard and a trend are different products that happen to look similar. A leaderboard answers "what is biggest," which is a question with a stable and slightly boring answer. A trend answers "what is moving," which is the question developers actually care about, and answering it well requires memory that a single live list does not have. Once I framed the build around movement instead of totals, the snapshot stopped being a convenience and became the core mechanism, because owning the data over time is the only way to show change over time. That reframing is the whole reason the dashboard is worth opening instead of just visiting GitHub's own trending page.

You can explore the full thing at [GitHub Trending Pulse](/github-trending-pulse). The quickest way to understand it is to scan a couple of language segments, then a topic segment, and pay attention to the weekly movement next to each repository rather than its raw star count, because that movement is the entire point of the project.

---


### Building a BART Dashboard That Answers One Question: Is a Train Coming

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/building-a-bart-transit-dashboard
- Published: 2026-06-15
- Topic: Civic Data
- Excerpt: I built Bay Area Transit Pulse to put the line map, per-station departures, and service alerts on one screen instead of three separate apps. Here is the build.

If you want to see the product before reading the breakdown, open [Bay Area Transit Pulse](/bay-area-transit).

When you are standing on a platform or deciding whether to leave the house, you are really only asking one thing, which is whether a train is coming and when. It sounds trivial, and yet getting that answer reliably usually means bouncing between three different surfaces. You check a route map to remember which line you need, you open a station page to see the next departures, and you go hunting in a separate alerts feed to find out whether anything is broken today. None of those three share a view, and none of them tell you the whole story on their own. I built Bay Area Transit Pulse to collapse that bouncing into a single screen.

## The question is simple, the answer is scattered

BART, like most transit systems, publishes plenty of data. The problem has never been availability. The problem is that the data lives in pieces that were designed to be consumed separately. The line map answers "which train," the departure board answers "when," and the advisories answer "is anything wrong," but a rider in a hurry needs all three at once and gets them one tab at a time. That fragmentation is annoying on a normal day and genuinely costly on a bad one, because the moment service is disrupted is exactly the moment you most need the map, the departures, and the alert in the same glance, and that is the moment the scattered design fails you hardest.

So the dashboard puts them together. It is organized around three views, a lines view that shows the system and how stations connect to the routes that serve them, a stations view that is a real departure board for any station you pick, and an advisories view that surfaces active service alerts and elevator outages in one place. The route state is deep-linkable, so the view you are on and the station you have selected live in the URL. A link to "Embarcadero departures" is just a link with the station abbreviation in it, like embr, which means you can bookmark your home station and land on its board directly. For a tool you use on a phone while walking, that kind of direct linking is not a nicety, it is the whole point.

## Pulling the whole system in one pass

BART exposes a public legacy API that does not even require you to register, because the agency publishes a working demo key, and I baked that key straight into the builder. The builder does a fair amount of stitching to produce a coherent snapshot. It pulls the full station list, then the routes and per-route info, which it uses to derive a station-to-lines mapping so the lines view actually knows which trains serve which stops. It pulls service advisories and elevator outages so the alerts view has something to show, and then it grabs real-time departures for every station in the system in a single call by asking for all origins at once. That last detail matters more than it sounds. Fetching departures station by station would mean dozens of requests and a slow, fragile build, whereas one call for the whole system keeps the pipeline fast and clean.

## The snapshot, plus a seed so it is never blank

The dashboard reads from a committed snapshot rather than calling BART at request time, which is the same pattern I use across this family of tools. A scheduled job refreshes it every six hours, regenerates the file, and commits it, and the running site only ever reads what has been committed. The refresh is conservative on purpose, so if a fetch fails or comes back thin, the script keeps the previous snapshot instead of replacing a good board with a broken one. Departure times are obviously the most perishable part of this data, which is the honest tradeoff of the snapshot approach, but the structure of the system, the stations, the lines, and the connections barely changes, and a steady, correct view of the network beats a live view that occasionally collapses.

The one thing I did differently here is that the snapshot ships with a hand-authored seed flagged as such, so the page is useful from the very first deploy, before any live refresh has run. An empty seed would have meant a blank dashboard until the first scheduled job fired, and for a transit tool that felt wrong. The seed gets replaced wholesale on the first real refresh, but it means the product is never showing nothing.

## What building it reinforced

Civic data is one of my favorite spaces to build in precisely because the agencies have already done the hard part of making the data public. What is so often missing is the small, opinionated layer on top that turns three feeds into one answer. Bay Area Transit Pulse does not generate any new information about BART. It just refuses to make the rider assemble the picture themselves. I think that is where a lot of the value in civic tech actually sits, not in novel data but in respecting the user's time enough to put the map, the departures, and the alerts where a person can read them together. The question was always simple. The work was making the answer simple too.

You can explore the full thing at [Bay Area Transit Pulse](/bay-area-transit). The quickest way to understand it is to open the lines view, pick a station to pull up its departure board, then check advisories to see whether anything is disrupted, all without leaving the page or losing your selection.

---


### Building SpaceX Mission Control to Turn Public Launch Data Into a Mission Board

- URL: https://isaacvazquez.com/writing/building-spacex-mission-control
- Published: 2026-04-02
- Topic: Product Design
- Excerpt: I built SpaceX Mission Control because most public API demos stop at retrieval. Here's what it took to turn flat launch data into a navigable, relationship-aware mission board.

If you want to try the product before reading the breakdown, open [SpaceX Mission Control](/spacex-mission-control).

Public APIs make it easy to access data. They do not automatically make that data feel usable. That gap is what this project explores. I wanted to turn public SpaceX launch data into something that felt closer to an operational board than a generic API demo. The result is a mission-control-style product with a clear next-launch focus, a browsable launch board, and deep-linked detail panels that stay aware of the relationships between launches, rockets, payloads, capsules, crew, and launch pads.

## The Problem With Most Public-Data Demos

A lot of public API projects stop at retrieval. Fetch a list, render a few cards, add filters, call it done. That proves the integration works, but it does not prove the product works.

For a subject like spaceflight, the data is inherently relational. A launch means more when you can connect it to the rocket, the orbit, the payloads, the pad, the crew, and the status of the mission itself. A flat list hides most of that richness. So the real product question became how you make public launch data feel navigable, operational, and worth exploring.

## Why The Experience Starts With The Next Launch

The first major decision was to center the interface on the next launch rather than treat all launches as equal. That mirrors how people naturally approach this category. Most users do not arrive asking for an abstract database browse. They want to know what is happening next, when it happens, and why it matters.

By giving the next launch a dedicated hero treatment, the product establishes a useful hierarchy, putting immediate mission awareness first, broader board browsing next, and deep detail exploration after that. This is a product-design decision, not just a layout decision. It tells the user where to start.

## The Core Product Decisions

The launch board is designed to feel like a working surface, not a passive archive. Upcoming and past launches can be filtered, scanned, and compared in a format that emphasizes operational status rather than generic content cards. That choice matters because launch data is inherently event-driven. A board structure makes the timeline and the state changes easier to grasp than a standard blog-style list.

One of the most important interaction decisions in the project is that mission detail is deep-linkable through route state. That means a specific launch and panel can be shared or revisited directly instead of existing only as transient UI state. It makes the experience more useful for exploration because the user can hold onto a meaningful point inside the product. Deep linking is often undervalued in dashboard-style projects. Here it matters because the detail panel is where the relationships between entities become legible.

The most important technical choice underneath the product is relationship-aware normalization. The UI should not make users think in raw API fragments. It should present a mission as a connected object, showing what rocket is involved, which payloads are attached, whether crew or capsules matter, where the mission launches, and how it fits into a larger launch story. That translation layer is what turns "API integration" into product behavior.

## Why This Needed To Feel Like A Product, Not A Showcase

Space-themed UI can become gimmicky very fast. I wanted this project to avoid that trap. The goal was not to make something that simply looked cinematic. The goal was to create a productized data experience where the interface hierarchy, the route state, and the data normalization all support a clearer understanding of the missions.

That required restraint, using visual atmosphere without sacrificing legibility, letting the mission data drive the interaction model, and keeping the detail layer useful rather than decorative. The style is part of the experience, but it is not the product by itself.

## What This Project Taught Me

Data products get stronger when they acknowledge the shape of the domain instead of forcing the domain into generic UI patterns. Spaceflight is event-driven, relationship-heavy, and status-sensitive. Once I treated those qualities as design inputs, the product got better quickly. The next-launch hero, the mission board, and the deep-linked detail panel all came out of respecting that structure.

This project also reinforced something I care about in dashboard design, which is that route state is part of usability. A view you can return to and share is more valuable than one that only exists in the current browser moment.

## Try The Live Product

You can explore the full experience at [SpaceX Mission Control](/spacex-mission-control). The best way to understand the product is to start with the next-launch hero, switch between upcoming and past launches, and then open a mission detail panel to see how the product turns separate API entities into one coherent mission view.
